newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Crucifix from Byzantine era found in Jerusalem.
newsitem.headline: Crucifix from Byzantine era found in Jerusalem.

text.p: A rare bronze-and-wood crucifix dating back to the Byzantine era was found during excavation work just outside the walls of the Old City in East Jerusalem, Israeli archaeologists said on Wednesday.
They cast doubt however on news reports the cross, discovered last week, contained wood from the original holy cross of Jesus.
They said the cross, which fits in the palm of one's hand, was a rare artifact because it was the first to be uncovered with wooden pieces in it dating back to the fifth and sixth centuries.

"The cross was found by a worker last week and this particular one is outstanding because it is made of bronze and inlaid with two pieces of wood," said Rony Reich, director of excavation at Israel's Antiquities Authority.
"But our small cross is not part of the holy cross," he told a news conference at the excavation site under a bridge just outside the walled Old City's Jaffa Gate.
He said many crosses were uncovered during their seven-year excavation at the site, but all were made of either bronze or stone.

Archaeologists at the Antiquities Authority said the crosses were found inside a building believed to have been an inn used by pilgrims, the largest neighbourhood just outside Jerusalem uncovered from the Byzantine period.
Reich said the excavations also uncovered a bath house and remains of shops dating back to the Byzantine period, between the 5th and 6th centuries.

Archaeologist Gideon Avni said the five-million dollar excavation project began in 1989 when construction of a major commercial project in Jerusalem's Mamilla neighbourhood revealed archaeological artifacts.
